pos: n. (the head of a family that returned from Babylon with Zerubbabel; later a sealer of the covenant)
etymology: Hebrew Betsai (H1209), perhaps the same word as H1153, of uncertain further derivation. The King James translators rendered it Bezai.
biblical_def: Bezai names a family head among the exiles who came up from Babylon with Zerubbabel and Jeshua: “The children of Bezai, three hundred twenty and three” (Ezra 2:17). Nehemiah’s register of the same company, drawn up independently, gives the household one man more: “The children of Bezai, three hundred twenty and four” (Nehemiah 7:23). The two censuses agree in every particular but the last digit, an honest discrepancy the compilers of Scripture did not smooth over — a household grows or is counted again by hand, and the record says so plainly rather than pretending to a false precision. The name resurfaces a generation later among those who bound Judah to a sure covenant after the wall was finished: “Now those that sealed were…Hodijah, Hashum, Bezai” (Nehemiah 10:1, 18). A family first known only by a number in a census list is, within the same book, known by a signature on a covenant document. The whole company is set in its frame at the opening of the list: “Now these are the children of the province that went up out of the captivity…and came again unto Jerusalem and Judah, every one unto his city” (Ezra 2:1).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for Bezai; the name belongs to a returning household counted twice, with a one-man difference between the two counts, and later to one of the sealers of Nehemiah’s covenant.
webster_full: BEZAI, n. The head of a family of Israelites who returned from Babylonian captivity.
CAPTIVITY, n. The state of being a prisoner, or of being in the power of an enemy by force or the fate of war.
COVENANT, n. A mutual agreement of two or more persons or parties, or a writing containing the terms of agreement.
SEAL, v.t. To fasten with a seal; to attest or confirm by a stamp, mark, or other visible sign.
REGISTER, n. A record; an account of proceedings or facts entered in a book.
scriptures: The children of Bezai, three hundred twenty and three.
The children of Bezai, three hundred twenty and four.

Now these are the children of the province that went up out of the captivity, of those which had been carried away, whom Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon had carried away unto Babylon, and came again unto Jerusalem and Judah, every one unto his city;
corruption_summary: A minor discrepancy of one man between two honest censuses is sometimes seized on by skeptics as proof against inerrancy, when it is exactly the opposite: two independent hand counts of the same living, growing household, both preserved without editorial harmonizing.
corruption_paragraphs: The historical-critical habit is to treat every numerical variance between Ezra 2 and Nehemiah 7 as evidence the lists cannot both be trustworthy, and from there to a general suspicion of the historical books as loosely edited folklore rather than administrative record. But a family of three hundred souls does not hold still between one census and the next; a birth, a death, a household absorbed or divided, and the number moves by one. The doctrine of inerrancy concerns what the original authors intended to assert, and Ezra and Nehemiah plainly intended to preserve two honest counts, not to harmonize them artificially — which is exactly what a true record of a living people looks like.

The name itself faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God counts His people by name and by household, not in the aggregate, and that the same man who is a number in a resettlement register can be found, a generation later, putting his name to a covenant. The exile did not dissolve Bezai’s house into an anonymous mass; it returned by name, was numbered by name, and at last signed by name.

“The children of Bezai, three hundred twenty and four” — the second count, one household grown by one.
“Hodijah, Hashum, Bezai” — the same name among those who sealed the covenant.

pos: n. (a family head who returned from Babylon; called Hariph in Nehemiah's parallel list)
etymology: Hebrew Yorah, from the root yarah (H3384), to cast, to teach, or connected to yoreh, the early autumn rain. Nehemiah’s parallel census gives the same household as Hariph, from choreph (H2779), autumn or harvest-time.
biblical_def: Two names, one household, the same exact number: Ezra’s register reads, “The children of Jorah, an hundred and twelve” (Ezra 2:18), and Nehemiah’s parallel register, drawn from an independent copy of the same archive, reads, “The children of Hariph, an hundred and twelve” (Nehemiah 7:24). The count matching to the man across two different scribal traditions is itself strong evidence that Jorah and Hariph name the identical family, whether by an ancestor’s two names, a place of origin, or a scribal preference for one form over the other — the corpus does not resolve the question and neither does this entry, but it does not need to; both names carried the same seventy-generations-later company home. The Hariph form reappears among those who set their name to Nehemiah’s covenant: “The priests…Malluch, Harim, Baanah…Hariph, Anathoth, Nebai” (Nehemiah 10:19). A household counted twice under two names and sealed once under one is a small but real witness to how carefully these records were kept, not how carelessly.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for Jorah; the household appears in Ezra’s list under this name and in Nehemiah’s parallel list as Hariph, both counts agreeing at one hundred and twelve.
webster_full: JORAH, n. The head of a family of Israelites who returned from Babylon; called Hariph in the parallel register.
AUTUMN, n. The third season of the year, between summer and winter, the time of harvest.
REGISTER, n. A written account or roll of persons, transactions, or events.
PARALLEL, a. Corresponding in every particular; having the same direction or course.
COVENANT, n. An agreement solemnly ratified between parties.
scriptures: The children of Jorah, an hundred and twelve.
The children of Hariph, an hundred and twelve.
So the priests, and the Levites, and some of the people, and the singers, and the porters, and the Nethinims, dwelt in their cities, and all Israel in their cities.
corruption_summary: A name that changes form between two parallel lists is sometimes read as confusion in the text; the matching headcount across both forms argues the opposite — careful, independent transmission of one true record.
corruption_paragraphs: The historical-critical instinct treats every variant spelling between Ezra and Nehemiah as a seam exposing careless redaction, stitched together from disagreeing sources long after the events. But a redactor inventing or garbling a name would have little reason to preserve the identical number, one hundred and twelve, across both forms; the number is the kind of detail that survives only where two witnesses are independently accurate about the same underlying record, not where one is copying the other's error.

The name itself faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the LORD's providence over His remnant is exact enough to be counted twice and come out the same, under two different names, in two different books. What men might call a discrepancy is, read rightly, a confirmation.

pos: n. (a family head who returned from Babylon; called by the place-name Gibeon in Nehemiah's parallel list)
etymology: Hebrew Gibbar (H1402), an intensive form of H1399, gever, a mighty man. The King James translators rendered it Gibbar in Ezra; Nehemiah's parallel list has the town-name Gibeon at the corresponding place.
biblical_def: Gibbar heads a household of ninety-five in Ezra’s roll of the return: “The children of Gibbar, ninety and five” (Ezra 2:20). At the identical place in Nehemiah’s independent register the same ninety-five are named not by ancestor but by town: “The children of Gibeon, ninety and five” (Nehemiah 7:25). This entry is on the ancestral name; it is distinct from the great and ancient city of Gibeon itself, whose treaty with Joshua and whose high place fill many chapters of the history — the census household is most naturally read as men who had settled at Gibeon and so came to be called after their town rather than their forefather, the two registers simply choosing different handles for the one family. The name Gibbar itself carries its own quiet irony: it is built on the Hebrew word for a mighty man, gever, the same root behind gibborim, the mighty men of David’s wars. The mighty man’s house did not return as an army; it returned as ninety-five names on a list, resettled “every one unto his city” (Ezra 2:1) among “all Israel in their cities” (Ezra 2:70).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for Gibbar; the name is built on the Hebrew word for a mighty man, and the household it names is counted at ninety-five in Ezra and given the town-name Gibeon at the same place in Nehemiah.
webster_full: GIBBAR, n. The head of a family of ninety-five Israelites who returned from Babylonian captivity.
MIGHTY, a. Possessing might or great bodily strength; powerful; strong.
CENSUS, n. An official enumeration of the inhabitants of a country, with details.
RESETTLE, v.t. To settle again; to establish anew in a place of former abode.
REMNANT, n. That which remains after a part is separated, removed, or destroyed.

So the priests, and the Levites, and some of the people, and the singers, and the porters, and the Nethinims, dwelt in their cities, and all Israel in their cities.
corruption_summary: A household named by ancestor in one census and by town in the parallel census is sometimes read as two rival, irreconcilable traditions; it is the ordinary way a settled family comes to be known by its place rather than only by its forebear.
corruption_paragraphs: Source-critical readings that carve Ezra and Nehemiah into competing, poorly harmonized traditions find a favorite exhibit in exactly this kind of pairing, where a personal name in one list stands opposite a place name in the other at the identical position with the identical number. But the identical count of ninety-five across both forms is the very thing such a theory cannot easily explain; two unrelated, badly stitched traditions do not independently arrive at the same figure. The simpler and more honest reading is that one family was known both ways, as families still are.

The name itself faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the mighty man’s house, after seventy years in Babylon, did not come home mighty in the world’s sense; it came home ninety-five souls, resettled among a remnant. Strength before God is not measured by the number a clan can field but by whether it answers, generations later, to its own name at all.

pos: n. (a man of Judah; also a family of Nethinim who returned from Babylon, one of whose sons repaired the Old Gate)
etymology: Hebrew Pase'ach, from pasach (H6452), to limp, to pass over, to hop; the same root that gives Pesach, Passover. Nehemiah’s Nethinim list spells the family name Phaseah at the corresponding place.
biblical_def: The name belongs first to a man of Judah in the Chronicler’s genealogy: “And Eshton begat Bethrapha, and Paseah, and Tehinnah the father of Irnahash. These are the men of Rechah” (1 Chronicles 4:12). A family bearing the same name is counted among the Nethinim, the temple servants, who returned with Zerubbabel: “The children of Uzza, the children of Paseah, the children of Besai” (Ezra 2:49). At the same place in Nehemiah’s independent register the family is spelled Phaseah: “The children of Gazzam, the children of Uzza, the children of Phaseah” (Nehemiah 7:51). A son of this returned house did not stay a name on a list; he took up a trowel: “Moreover the old gate repaired Jehoiada the son of Paseah, and Meshullam the son of Besodeiah” (Nehemiah 3:6). The name’s own root, pasach, to limp or to pass over, is the same verb behind Pesach, the Passover, the night the LORD passed over the houses marked by blood. A family named from limping and passing over spent its strength, generations later, rebuilding the very gates of the city the LORD had once passed over in judgment and mercy both.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for Paseah; the name is built on the Hebrew verb for limping or passing over, the same root behind Passover, and belongs to a man of Judah and to a family of Nethinim whose son helped rebuild Jerusalem’s wall.

NETHINIM, n. Temple servants given by the congregation of Israel to assist the Levites.

corruption_summary: The two spellings, Paseah and Phaseah, are sometimes cited as evidence of an unreliable text; read plainly they are ordinary orthographic variation within a single language across two independently copied books, exactly as the same name is spelled two ways in a modern family Bible's flyleaf.
corruption_paragraphs: A skeptical reading of the historical books treats every spelling difference as a wound in the text’s reliability, building toward the conclusion that Scripture cannot be trusted in its details because it is not perfectly uniform in its details. But perfect uniformity of spelling was never the promise; verbal plenary inspiration guarantees that what the human authors wrote down was exactly what the Spirit intended asserted, and two faithful scribes rendering one Hebrew name with or without an initial letter is precisely the kind of variation that honest, independent transmission produces.

The name itself faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is in the root: a name built on limping and on passing over became, in Jehoiada son of Paseah, a name attached to a repaired gate. The LORD who passed over Israel in Egypt is the same LORD whose gates a limping people’s sons were given strength to rebuild.

pos: n. (a family of Nethinim who returned from Babylon)
etymology: Hebrew Besai (H1153), from bus (H947), to tread down, hence domineering; a name the lexicons class among the Nethinim, the temple servants.
biblical_def: Besai names one household among the Nethinim, the temple servants, who returned with Zerubbabel and Jeshua: “The children of Uzza, the children of Paseah, the children of Besai” (Ezra 2:49). Nehemiah’s independent register preserves the family at the identical place in the list: “The children of Besai, the children of Meunim, the children of Nephishesim” (Nehemiah 7:52). Strong’s Hebrew concordance connects the name to a root meaning to tread down or domineer, an odd inheritance for a family whose whole recorded history is one of humble, treading service — hewing wood and drawing water for the house of the LORD, not ruling over anyone. Scripture does not explain the name; it simply preserves it, twice, in two hands, among the servants who made the sacrifices possible without ever offering one themselves. The frame around the whole list states what such service was for: the exiles came again unto Jerusalem, “every one unto his city” (Ezra 2:1), and at the end, “all Israel in their cities” (Nehemiah 7:73), a servant people settled at last in a land of their own.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for Besai; the Hebrew root is connected to treading down, and the name belongs to a family of Nethinim, the temple servants who returned from Babylon.
webster_full: BESAI, n. The head of a family of Nethinim, or temple servants, who returned from Babylonian captivity.
SERVANT, n. A person who attends another for the purpose of performing menial offices for him.
TEMPLE, n. A public edifice erected in honor of some deity; among the Jews, the house of God at Jerusalem.
MENIAL, a. Pertaining to servants; low; mean; servile.
NETHINIM, n. Those given; temple servants assigned to assist the Levites in their duties.

So the priests, and the Levites, and the porters, and the singers, and some of the people, and the Nethinims, and all Israel, dwelt in their cities; and when the seventh month came, the children of Israel were in their cities.
corruption_summary: A name meaning to tread down or domineer is sometimes read into a portrait of the man himself; Scripture gives no such portrait, and the safer reading refuses to build a character study on an etymology the text itself does not develop.
corruption_paragraphs: It is a modern temptation, especially online where every name is run through an etymology dictionary for personality content, to construct a moral or psychological reading of an ancient figure purely from what his name is thought to mean, as though Hebrew parents in exile named their sons as horoscopes. Scripture resists this discipline everywhere the name-bearer’s own life is unrecorded: it gives the name, the number, the service, and stops.

The name itself faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the dignity of unrecorded service. Besai’s house left no deed, no speech, no single named man beyond the family head — only a place among the Nethinim, those given to the temple’s daily, unglamorous labor. The LORD who numbers the hairs of every head numbered this house too, by name, twice.

pos: n. (a family of Nethinim who returned from Babylon; spelled Mehunim in Ezra's register; not to be confused with the Arabian people of the same root fought by King Uzziah)
etymology: Hebrew Me'unim / Mehunim, likely a gentilic from Ma'on, dwelling-place; the same consonantal root as the hostile Arabian tribe called the Mehunims in Chronicles, though the two are distinct peoples.
biblical_def: One household of Nethinim returning from Babylon bears this name: Ezra’s register spells it “The children of Asnah, the children of Mehunim, the children of Nephusim” (Ezra 2:50), and Nehemiah’s independent register at the same place gives “The children of Besai, the children of Meunim, the children of Nephishesim” (Nehemiah 7:52). The name shares its Hebrew root with a very different company: “And God helped him against the Philistines, and against the Arabians that dwelt in Gurbaal, and the Mehunims” (2 Chronicles 26:7), a hostile Arabian people King Uzziah fought and subdued. Scripture never confuses the two; the Chronicler places the Arabian Mehunims among Judah’s enemies and the Nethinim household among the LORD’s own temple servants, and this entry keeps them just as distinct. The same consonants can name a people at war with the covenant and a family serving inside it, which is itself a small witness that a name, even a dangerous one, does not fix a house’s destiny before the LORD. This particular house was counted home among “all Israel in their cities” (Ezra 2:70), not among the nations it happened to share a root-word with.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for Meunim; the same Hebrew root names both a family of returning Nethinim and, in Chronicles, an unrelated Arabian people fought by King Uzziah — two distinct entities the text itself never confuses.
webster_full: MEUNIM, n. A family of Nethinim, or temple servants, who returned from Babylonian captivity; spelled Mehunim in Ezra.

corruption_summary: A shared Hebrew root between a servant household and a hostile Arabian people is sometimes flattened into a single confused entity by careless popular reference works; the biblical text keeps the two entirely distinct and so does sound lexicography.
corruption_paragraphs: Popular online Bible-name dictionaries frequently merge every occurrence of a shared consonantal root into one undifferentiated article, producing the impression that the Nethinim family and Uzziah’s Arabian enemies were somehow the same people or that the text is confused about who they were. This is carelessness with the historical narrative, not a discovery about it; the Chronicler is perfectly clear that one is a covenant household inside Jerusalem and the other a foreign power God subdued through Judah’s king.

The name itself faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is precision in handling a shared root: two peoples can carry the same word in their name and stand on opposite sides of the covenant. Grace, not etymology, determines which side of that line a house is found on, and this house is found among the returned and resettled remnant.

pos: n. (a family of Nethinim who returned from Babylon; spelled Nephishesim in Nehemiah's parallel register)
etymology: Hebrew Nephusim, likely from puts (H6327), to scatter, to disperse; Nehemiah's register spells the same family Nephishesim.
biblical_def: This household closes out a section of the Nethinim register in Ezra: “The children of Asnah, the children of Mehunim, the children of Nephusim” (Ezra 2:50). Nehemiah’s independently kept parallel gives the family a slightly different spelling at the identical place: “The children of Besai, the children of Meunim, the children of Nephishesim” (Nehemiah 7:52). The likeliest root behind the name is the Hebrew verb puts, to scatter or disperse — a fitting name, whatever its exact derivation, for a household counted among a people who had themselves been scattered among the nations and were now, list by list, family by family, being gathered home again. The two spellings across the two books are not treated by either author as requiring correction; each simply records the name as his own source preserved it, and both agree the household belonged among the Nethinim who returned. The frame around the whole census makes the point without needing to state it: those once scattered “came again unto Jerusalem and Judah, every one unto his city” (Ezra 2:1).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for Nephusim; the likely Hebrew root means to scatter or disperse, a fitting name for a household of a once-scattered people counted among those who returned.

corruption_summary: Two spellings of one obscure household name are the kind of variant that invites a dismissive verdict on the text's reliability; read within the whole chapter it is a minor, honestly preserved detail inside an otherwise precisely matching record.
corruption_paragraphs: Where a name is rare enough that most readers have never encountered it, a critical commentary can spend disproportionate energy treating its spelling variance as evidence of textual corruption in the technical, manuscript-critical sense, implying the underlying record is unstable. The stronger and simpler explanation, consistent with the rest of the chapter, is ordinary transliteration variance in the scribal tradition of a name neither author needed to standardize for his purpose.

The name itself faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the reversal the name itself may quietly picture: a household once scattered is, in the very sentence that names it, found gathered again among the returning remnant. Scattering was Babylon’s sentence; gathering was the LORD’s mercy, and both are held in one small, easily overlooked name.

The name is not invented for the family; it is the ordinary Hebrew word for an earthen bottle or flask, the same word the prophet uses when the LORD sends him to buy a potter’s vessel and break it before the elders as a sign of judgment on a hardened people. Whatever occasion first gave this household its name, Scripture is content simply to record it among the servants of the temple, without further comment, alongside a frame that says why the whole list matters: exiles “came again unto Jerusalem and Judah, every one unto his city” (Ezra 2:1), and at the end, “all Israel in their cities” (Ezra 2:70).

corruption_paragraphs: Skeptical popular treatments of obscure biblical names delight in pointing out that some mean nothing more exalted than household objects, as though this proves the genealogies are late invention rather than sober record-keeping. But real households in every culture and century have borne names drawn from trades, objects, and circumstances rather than theological statements; the very plainness of a name like Bakbuk is a mark of authenticity, not embarrassment.

The name itself faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the LORD who once sent a prophet to break an earthen bottle as a sign of judgment also received, in mercy, a whole household named for that same common vessel back into His temple’s service. Judgment and restoration can be spoken in the very same plain Hebrew word.

biblical_def: Hakupha names a family of Nethinim listed between two other returning households in both censuses of the return: “The children of Bakbuk, the children of Hakupha, the children of Harhur” (Ezra 2:51), matched word for word in Nehemiah’s independent register, “The children of Bakbuk, the children of Hakupha, the children of Harhur” (Nehemiah 7:53). Older lexicons connect the name to a Hebrew root meaning bent or bowed down, though Scripture attaches no story to the meaning; it simply preserves the family among the Nethinim, the servants given to assist the Levites in the daily work of the temple. A name that may mean bent belongs, in the record, to a household that was not broken by seventy years in Babylon — bent, perhaps, but not destroyed, and carried home again to serve at the very house of God it had been exiled from. The census frame states the outcome plainly: they “came again unto Jerusalem and Judah, every one unto his city” (Ezra 2:1), and were at last counted among “all Israel in their cities” (Nehemiah 7:73).

corruption_summary: A name understood to mean bent or bowed is sometimes pressed into a shame-narrative by modern popular sources eager to psychoanalyze ancient households; Scripture offers no such reading and none is warranted.
corruption_paragraphs: It has become common in casual online name-meaning sites to attach a modern emotional narrative — brokenness, low self-worth, generational trauma — to any biblical name whose root suggests bending or bowing, projecting therapeutic categories backward onto people the text never describes in those terms. The text records a household, a number, and a place in a list; it does not offer a psychological biography, and neither should its readers invent one.

The name itself faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that bowing, in Scripture’s own vocabulary, is most often the posture of worship rather than shame — the same body that bends before the LORD in humble service is the body He raises up. A household possibly named for bending was, in fact, restored to bow again at the house of God.

etymology: Hebrew Charchur, a reduplicated form of charah (H2734), to burn, to be kindled; suggesting fever or inflammation.
biblical_def: Harhur closes the same short group of three household names in both censuses of the return: “The children of Bakbuk, the children of Hakupha, the children of Harhur” (Ezra 2:51), preserved word for word in Nehemiah’s independent register, “The children of Bakbuk, the children of Hakupha, the children of Harhur” (Nehemiah 7:53). The name is built on a doubled Hebrew root for burning or kindling, the same root that describes anger kindled in a man or fire kindled on an altar; whether the household’s ancestor was named for a fever, a temperament, or some other cause, Scripture records only the name and the number, one household among the Nethinim given to serve the temple. Set beside its neighbors Bakbuk and Hakupha, a bottle and a bending, Harhur completes a small cluster of plain, homely Hebrew names — nothing exalted, nothing invented for effect — exactly what a real administrative census of real families looks like. The frame around them all is the point: they “came again unto Jerusalem and Judah, every one unto his city” (Ezra 2:70), and were counted among “all Israel in their cities” (Nehemiah 7:73).

corruption_summary: A name built on a root for burning or fever invites speculative medical or emotional backstory from modern readers; the text supplies none, and sound handling of Scripture does not supply what the text withholds.
corruption_paragraphs: The temptation with a name like this, once its root meaning is known, is to write the household a biography the text never gives — an ancestor who nearly died of fever, a family temperament of burning anger, and so on. This is the same interpretive overreach that turns a bare genealogy into speculative fiction; the discipline of honest exposition is to say plainly what the text says and no more.

The name itself faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is restraint before a silent text, paired with confidence in what is not silent: this household, whatever burned in its history, was carried through captivity and set down again in its own city, one more small proof that the LORD who kindles judgment also kindles mercy for a remnant that returns.
